blocks.text: A systems-oriented choice has consequences outside a single calculation. Selecting a buffer size can affect memory use. Keeping a file open can prevent another operation. topics.title: 1.1.2 Understanding Where C++ Is Used in Industry
topics.summary: C++ is useful when software must combine abstraction with explicit control over representation, resource lifetime, and execution costs. Examples include native applications, game engines, embedded software, numerical libraries, storage systems, and network services. These examples describe workload families, not a promise that one language is automatically the right choice for every project.

blocks.text: The useful question is not “Is C++ fast?” but “Which requirements make its control valuable here?” A device application might need access to an existing C or C++ library. A numerical program might need a representation that avoids unnecessary data movement. A desktop application might need to reuse a mature native component. These are different reasons to choose the same language; none establishes that every program should be written in it.

This is also how you resist premature optimization: you keep the actual workload, not an imagined future machine, at the center of the decision.

reading.title: 1.2.2 Combining Object Files Through Linking
paragraphs: An object file contains machine code and metadata, including references to functions or objects that may be defined elsewhere. The linker combines compatible object files and libraries, resolves those references, and constructs an executable or library. A declaration can allow compilation to succeed while a missing definition causes linking to fail.

For example, int total(); tells the compiler how a call is formed. It does not provide the function body. When separate files define and call total, both relevant object files must participate in the link. Link order, library search paths, and binary compatibility become important later. For now, distinguish a source-level name error from a linker message such as an undefined reference.

An object file can contain machine instructions while still depending on definitions supplied elsewhere. Imagine one source file calling a function named groups_needed and another source file defining it. The first compiler invocation can check the call if it sees a compatible declaration. The linker later has to find the definition among the supplied objects and libraries.

This gives two different questions. Compilation asks whether the translation unit is acceptable under the chosen rules. Linking asks whether the program’s required definitions can be assembled into the requested artifact. A successful compile-only command answers the first question, not the second. Running g++ -c and finding no executable is therefore expected, not a mysterious installation failure.

cards.question: Can a source file exist without any executable?
cards.answer: Yes. Editing and saving text does not invoke translation. The first evidence of a build is a tool invocation and its outputs.

cards.question: Can an object file be correct while linking fails?
cards.answer: Yes. A translation unit may be acceptable but require a definition not supplied to the linker. Correctness at one stage does not imply completeness at the next.

cards.question: Does a successful run prove the source currently open in the editor was built?
cards.answer: No. You must connect the source path and timestamp or content to a successful build of the executable you launched. The stale-executable experiment demonstrates why.

cards.question: Must every C++20 program use new C++20 features?
cards.answer: No. A baseline permits a language feature set; it does not require every available feature in every program.

cards.question: Why keep generated files in a build directory?
cards.answer: It separates replaceable artifacts from authored source. You can remove and regenerate build outputs without deleting the work you are trying to preserve. That directory boundary becomes a practical recovery mechanism throughout the book.

cards.question: What changes when you save main.cpp?
cards.answer: Only source text on disk changes. An executable changes after a successful build. Run the newly built file to check the change.

cards.question: What job does preprocessing do?
cards.answer: It handles directives such as #include and conditional compilation before later translation stages. Included declarations become part of the translation unit.

cards.question: What does a compiler check that an editor may miss?
cards.answer: It checks actual code under the selected language mode, including types and declarations. Syntax coloring is not proof that a build succeeds.

cards.question: What is an object file missing before linking?
cards.answer: It may still have references to definitions in other object files or libraries. Linking resolves those references and combines the required pieces.

cards.question: A source file compiles, but add() is undefined at link time. Where should you look?
cards.answer: Look for the missing definition, a signature mismatch, or an object file omitted from the link command. Rewriting the caller's arithmetic will not supply the missing symbol.

cards.question: Why can an old executable print output after a failed build?
cards.answer: A failed build may leave the previous executable in place. Its output describes the previous successful build, not the changed source.

cards.question: What does -std=c++20 select?
cards.answer: It selects a compiler's C++20 language mode. Compiler and standard-library support must still be checked for features you actually use.

cards.question: Does __cplusplus identify the operating system?
cards.answer: No. It reports a language-version tag. It does not describe the operating system, processor, or every supported library feature.

cards.question: How do compilation and execution differ?
cards.answer: Compilation translates and checks source. Execution runs the resulting program on input. A valid translation can still contain a wrong algorithm.

cards.question: Why keep a reading's identifier and value in one record when sorting?
cards.answer: Moving the record keeps those fields together. Sorting a separate identifier array can attach measurements to the wrong identifiers.

cards.question: What must a sort comparison using integer identifiers promise?
cards.answer: It must define a strict weak ordering. Using < works for these identifiers; using <= incorrectly says a value precedes itself.

cards.question: What evidence connects observed output to a particular source change?
cards.answer: Record the source revision, exact build command, successful exit status, executable path, input, and output. Each item closes a different gap in the evidence trail.

cards.question: What must std::string stageName(int stage) accept and reject?
cards.answer: Map 0 to preprocess, 1 to compile, 2 to assemble, and 3 to link. Return invalid for any other integer. This models stage labels; it does not run a compiler.

focus.title: Keep related data together
explain: struct defines a value type named Reading. Each value contains an integer id and a double value.
main is the program’s entry point. The opening brace begins its body.
vector owns its Reading elements. The nested braces construct three complete readings, so sorting moves each id and value together.
focus.what: A Reading is one record. The vector owns a collection of these records.
focus.where: The records are created before sorting.
focus.why: Separate arrays for ids and values would need perfectly matched swaps. One value type keeps related fields together.
focus.invariant: Each id remains attached to its original measurement. The vector stays alive during sorting and printing.
focus.risk: Sorting ids alone would detach them from the matching values.

focus.title: Order, then borrow each result
focus.code:
std::sort(r.begin(), r.end(), [](const Reading& a, const Reading& b){ return a.id < b.id; });
    for (const auto& x : r) std::cout << x.id << ':' << x.value << '\n';
explain: sort receives an iterator pair marking a half-open range. The lambda, a small unnamed function, takes const references: it borrows two records without changing them and returns whether the first id is smaller.
The colon in this range-based for means “take each element from r.” auto lets the compiler find Reading; const & borrows it for read-only access. << inserts values into the output stream.
focus.what: The algorithm changes the order of values; the loop observes the resulting order.
focus.where: Both lines run after construction and before the vector is destroyed at the end of main.
focus.why: The comparator states one rule that the library sorting algorithm can apply repeatedly.
focus.invariant: The comparator must provide a strict weak ordering. Using < on these integer ids satisfies that rule.
focus.risk: Using <= breaks the ordering contract. Keeping a reference after the vector dies would leave a dangling reference.
